title: The Arithmetic of Power
location: Finance Ministry — Conference Room, Aldric Street

narrative.text: The Finance Ministry conference room has not been renovated since 1952. The carpet is a particular shade of governmental green that has not existed outside of public buildings for a decade. The overhead lights buzz slightly — a sound you stop hearing after the first hour, which is probably why meetings here always run long. Elara Vostane is showing Gregor Marić a chart. He is not looking at the chart.
The numbers are not a matter of opinion.
The numbers are not the question.
They are always the question.
They are never the only question.

Vostane does not respond. The silence is longer than usual for her — long enough that it registers as an argument rather than a pause. She sees you in the doorway. Her posture shifts almost imperceptibly. Relief. Or the closest thing to it that a woman like Vostane permits herself.
Chancellor. Shall we begin.
Not a question. The door closes behind you.
The deficit is structural. Cutting welfare won't fix it — will just make it quieter.

Quieter? Listen. Come to Kravenstal this winter, Elara. Walk down Ostrov Street in February and count the chimneys that are not smoking because the families inside cannot afford coal. Count them. Then come back to this conference room and tell me the deficit is quieter. These people don't hear budget projections. They hear their children coughing in the cold.
I am telling it to the Chancellor's budget projections, Gregor. The numbers do not negotiate.

The door opens. You enter. Both ministers turn — Vostane with the controlled expression of someone who was mid-argument and intends to resume it, Marić with the raw-throated frustration of someone who has been arguing for an hour already and is only now being heard.

The Finance Ministry conference room has not been renovated since 1952. The carpet is a particular shade of governmental green that has not existed outside of public buildings for a decade. Elara Vostane requested this meeting here rather than at the palace, and you did not ask why. You understand why: she wants you making decisions in a room that feels like a spreadsheet rather than a throne room. She is probably correct that the room matters.

The rear wall has been converted into a projection surface. The national budget fills it from floor to ceiling: revenues, expenditures, the gap between them laid out in columns so clean they could be mistaken for certainty. Vyktor Reznik sits to your left. He has been reviewing these numbers for three days and he looks like it.

Revenue: 380 million Krone. Expenditure: 445 million. The deficit is 65 million per annum, compounding annually against a national debt already at 340 million. If we maintain current spending levels for 4 years, debt service alone will consume 20 percent of revenue. That is before we discuss the maintenance backlog, the pension liability, or what happens to our credit rating if the IMA revises their assessment.

The military consumes 120 million. Debt service: 75. Government administration: 65. Infrastructure maintenance: 55. Education: 45. Healthcare: 40. Welfare: 25. BNI and internal security: 20 million for a service that does not officially exist. Every line item has a constituency. Every cut has a cost. The question is not whether someone suffers — the question is who.

She is correct and she knows she's correct and the correctness is the point. There is a particular kind of power in being the person who controls the numbers, because the numbers make every argument look like arithmetic when most of them are actually choices about who matters.
I've modeled 4 scenarios. I'll give you the honest version of each, not the political version. Vyktor can give you the political version afterward.

First: austerity. We cut 70 million from expenditure — primarily welfare, infrastructure deferral, and BNI dissolution. Deficit eliminated in 18 months. Debt service becomes sustainable. The IMA calls this the responsible scenario. The workers of Kravenstal call it something else. Unemployment rises during the adjustment period. Social unrest increases. We get fiscal sustainability at the cost of social stability — and potentially the government itself.

Second: revenue reform. We raise the corporate tax rate and introduce a wealth tier on incomes above 40,000 Krone. Revenue increases by 40 million. We still need to cut 25 million, but the burden shifts upward. Capital flight risk is real — I estimate 8 to 15 percent of business investment leaves within the year. The business community will treat this as a declaration of war. The workers will treat it as a promise kept.

Third: foreign credit. The IMA will extend a bridge loan — I've had preliminary conversations. 80 million at 6.5 percent, tied to a structural adjustment program. We buy 4 years of fiscal breathing room. In exchange, we accept IMA oversight of the budget process and specific mandated reforms: privatization of the steel sector, reduction of welfare expenditure, elimination of agricultural subsidies. We get time. We lose control.

Fourth: growth investment. We maintain the deficit and redirect 40 million toward infrastructure and industrial modernization. The theory is growth pays down debt faster than cuts. I've seen this work in 3 countries and fail in 11. It requires exactly the policy stability and investor confidence we do not currently possess. I'm not recommending this scenario. I'm telling you it exists.

Political translation: austerity loses Kravenstal in the next election. Revenue reform loses the business community for a decade. Foreign credit gives the IMA a seat at your cabinet table. Growth investment requires you to be correct about economic fundamentals. I am not competent to evaluate that.

The room is quiet. The budget projection covers the wall. Elara Vostane is watching you without expression — she has presented four paths and she will implement whichever you choose with equal professional precision. Vyktor is watching the table. The numbers are real. The people behind them are real. The choice is yours.

monologue: Vostane has turned the rear wall into a projection surface. The national budget fills it from floor to ceiling — revenues, expenditures, the gap between them laid out in columns so clean they could be mistaken for certainty. Four scenarios. Four different futures. She will implement whichever I choose with equal professional precision. The room is a spreadsheet, not a throne room. She chose it deliberately. Probably correct that the room matters.

choices.text: "Austerity. We cannot build on an unstable foundation. Cut spending to eliminate the deficit, absorb the political cost now, and create conditions for growth from a position of fiscal stability. I'll own it."

reactions.text: That is not a strategy. That is a position.
He starts to speak. He stops. He looks at the table.

choices.text: "Revenue reform. The workers didn't create this deficit — they shouldn't absorb it. Raise the corporate rate, introduce the wealth tier. We may lose some investment, but we keep the social contract."

reactions.text: The tension in his shoulders releases all at once.
He notes something in his folder. You cannot see what.

choices.text: "The IMA loan. I don't like the conditionality but we need time more than we need clean hands on the budget. Negotiate the best terms available and use the four years to grow our way to a better position."

reactions.text: I will initiate contact with the IMA mission chief this afternoon. The structural adjustment conditions will arrive within forty-eight hours. We should prepare the public messaging before the opposition frames it as surrender.
Foreign credit. He rubs his temples with both hands. The IMA does not lend money, he says quietly. It lends instructions. His father told him that. His father was right about many things.

choices.text: "Growth investment. We maintain the deficit and direct the capital toward the sectors that can generate returns — infrastructure, industrial modernization, education. This only works if it works, and I'm betting it will."

reactions.text: The people in Kravenstal won't feel that for two years.
